Source R1. No 479. Oct 19th, 1942

The Constructivists' Club.

This club held a meeting on Sunday, Oct 18th, on the premises of the Austria Office, where S. RETZLAW, alias Karl GROEHL gave a lecture on "The Situation in Germany." RETZLAW began by stating that the German nation was not enslaved by the Nazis, as shown by the fact that compulsion would not enable it to maintain such a prodigious war effort. Although many Germans wanted peace with Russia, they were not against war on principle, and the war with Britain was particularly popular. This did not imply that there was no opposition to Nazism, but there was no driving force in the anti-Nazis. Broadcasts from abroad were feeble and in any case listening in to foreign stations was on the decrease because it was impossible to replace wireless parts that wore out. The Germans needed wireless propaganda which would give them something to fight for, such as ideals of socialism and humanity, which they certainly would not get from London, which had no use for a German revolution, although it might have some for a counter-revolution. Consequently the German anti-Fascists in Britain must evolve their own programme and convey it to the German people, where in view of Germany's huge casualties and lack of decisive victories it would fall on fruitful soil, especially as air raids provoked wrath against Hitler because the Nazi authorities did not provide adequate shelter. In Bavaria and the Rhineland there were signs of a desire for peace and anger against Prussia and Berlin. In Hamburg, Bremen and other harbour towns there were outbursts of rage against the Nazis. Germany was short of railway transport, but the food situation was not desperate. Army rations were good. There was plenty of entertainment which made people forget their worries.

RETZLAW considered the entire German nation more or less responsible for Nazi atrocities and said they had got the government they deserved. But the emigrants had also to bear the blame, since a warmonger like Victor SCHIFF was on the SOPADE Committee in London, while GRZESINSKI and SOLLMANN were its spokesmen in the USA. "Die Zeitung" was edited by persons who would be Hitler's supporters if he had not thrown them out.
